summary: A language objective for ages 11-13: pupils become fluent in conventional geometric terms and notation (AB for segments, ∠ABC with the vertex as the middle letter, ∥ and arrows for parallel, the right-angle square for perpendicular, tick marks for equal lengths, and the vocabulary of regular polygons and their reflective/rotational symmetry) and USE them accurately to describe, sketch and draw figures. The goal is productive, property-based communication, not reciting definitions. The dominant obstacle is the prototype phenomenon: pupils who can state a correct definition still name shapes by their prototypical picture, so a tilted square is denied its name and 'parallel'/'perpendicular' get muddled or wrongly thought to require equal lengths. Effective teaching ties each term to its defining property (not its look), shows figures tilted, scaled and as non-examples, and gives pupils a reason to USE the notation through barrier/describe-and-draw tasks where imprecise language visibly breaks communication.
misconceptions: Prototype-driven naming: a shape is denied its name when tilted or non-standard (a 'slanted' square isn't called a square), even when the pupil knows the definition
Confusing or swapping 'parallel' and 'perpendicular', or believing parallel lines must be equal in length
Calling a polygon 'regular' when it has equal sides OR equal angles but not both (or just because it 'looks neat')
Writing ∠ABC with the vertex not in the middle, or naming an angle by a single letter where it is ambiguous
Using vague everyday words ('slanty line', 'pointy corner') instead of conventional terms and notation

activities.title: Barrier game: describe a figure so a partner can draw it
steps: Sit on one side of a barrier (screen, book, or divider) with a figure the partner cannot see: a tilted regular hexagon, a pair of parallel lines of clearly different lengths, and a perpendicular crossing

Describe the figure precisely enough that the unseen partner can reproduce it, naming which lines are parallel (∥ / arrows) and which are perpendicular (right-angle square), naming angles as ∠ABC with the vertex as the middle letter, and calling the hexagon 'regular' because its sides AND angles are equal
Place or speak the notation marks the partner needs — parallel arrows, right-angle squares, ∠ABC labels, equal-length tick marks
Compare the partner's drawing with the original and discuss where it diverged
Swap roles and repeat with a new figure
activities.insight: Precise words and marks make the drawing come out right while vague ones do not, so geometric language becomes a tool with consequences rather than a list to memorise.

activities.title: Label-and-rebuild: mark the notation and check it reconstructs
steps: Label a given figure on paper or screen using on-screen/drawn notation: ∥ arrows, right-angle squares, ∠ABC labels, 'regular', and equal-length tick marks
Have a partner (or an auto-drawer, if available) rebuild the figure from only your labels
Where the rebuild mismatches the original, find the misused term or misplaced mark and correct it
Deliberately include tilted shapes and unequal-length parallels so length and orientation errors show up
activities.insight: Notation is a precise instruction set: a mark in the wrong place or a term misused produces a different figure, so the marks carry real meaning.

activities.title: Defeat the prototype: name shapes by property across orientations
steps: Examine the same shape shown in many orientations (upright, tilted, rotated) and as near-miss non-examples
Decide and justify a name for each using the defining property — e.g. 'regular' only when sides AND angles are both equal — not its appearance

Compare a regular hexagon with an irregular polygon that has equal sides but unequal angles (e.g. a non-square rhombus), and separately with one that has equal angles but unequal sides (e.g. a non-square rectangle), and explain why neither of the latter two is regular
For a tilted square or hexagon, state that it keeps its name because the defining property still holds
Optionally tap a segment, angle, or line-pair in an interactive figure to reveal its correct term/notation (e.g. AB, ∠ABC with vertex B, ∥ or ⊥) and confirm a tilted square is still a square
activities.insight: A shape's name follows its defining properties, so orientation and scale do not change it, and 'regular' requires BOTH equal sides and equal angles — meeting only one condition is not enough.

activities.title: Symmetry by action: fold and rotate a regular polygon
steps: Take a cut-out regular hexagon (or other regular polygon) and fold it to find each line of reflective symmetry, counting them
Rotate the polygon over a fixed outline to find its order of rotational symmetry, counting the positions where it maps onto itself
State the result in conventional terms — e.g. a regular hexagon has 6 lines of reflective symmetry and rotational symmetry of order 6 — justified by the folding and rotating, not asserted
Optionally use rotation overlays or fold-line marks to record each symmetry found
activities.insight: Lines of symmetry and order of rotational symmetry are demonstrable facts about a figure, justified by physically folding and rotating rather than by memorised numbers.

activities.title: Match and categorise: receptive check with prototype distractors
steps: Match notation (∥, ⊥, ∠ABC) to the figure it describes, with distractors that swap parallel and perpendicular

Categorise polygons as regular or irregular, including a tilted regular hexagon and both an equal-sides-but-unequal-angles irregular polygon (non-square rhombus) and an equal-angles-but-unequal-sides irregular polygon (non-square rectangle)
Mark the right-angle and parallel symbols in a figure by drawing the symbol in the correct place
activities.insight: The learner can recognise correct terms and notation and distinguish regular from irregular even when the figure is tilted or a near-miss.

checkQuestion: Put a figure in front of the child — a tilted regular hexagon, a pair of parallel lines of clearly different lengths, and a perpendicular crossing. Say: 'Describe this figure to me precisely enough that I could draw it without seeing it — name the lines that are parallel and perpendicular, name the angles, and describe the hexagon and its symmetry.' Listen for how they USE the conventional terms and notation in context; do not ask them to define any word.
checkAnswer: Spontaneously and correctly uses conventional terms and notation in the description: names segments (AB), angles as ∠ABC with the vertex in the middle, states which lines are parallel (∥ / arrows) and which perpendicular (right-angle square), calls the hexagon 'regular' because its sides AND angles are equal (regardless of its tilt), and describes it as having 6 lines of reflective symmetry and rotational symmetry of order 6 — used in context to communicate, not recited as definitions.
